_comment: How each place of the catalogue's words-07.jsonl was settled before it went in config/figures-seen/: two readers read every place against its BSB verse, one asking whether the figure is plainly there and one whether the marked words, form and tags are right; a place both passed is kept as handed over, and any place either questioned was read a third time and kept, changed or dropped. A new form stands only where a reader proposed it. Places not read are held, not listed.

Then kept figures of speech were read again by two readers, a third settling any difference ("words re-read" counts them: those a sample showed at risk, such as wide spans, or those found only in the Hebrew or Greek that carry no tags): each kept as it was, cut to the words that carry the figure, or dropped ("words").

Last, a sample of 25 kept places was read by two more readers, a third settling any split; the file goes in only when 24 or more pass, and any place that fails is dropped. "samples" lists each sample and its result.

Strong's tags are also taken off any kept place whose tags light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, or whose roots light more words of the verse than there are tags, or, on a question or parallel lines, that were chosen for marked words since changed: such tags are a stretch of words, or name words no longer marked.
A place whose verse already has the same form from an earlier file is left out here, since the earlier file's place stands ("same form already on this verse").

places.why: "Will he not take hold of it and lift it out?" expects a plain yes, and 12:12 draws the point ("How much more valuable is a man than a sheep!"). The span started on a stray comma, so it now covers the whole question from "If one of you has a sheep".

The servants are puzzled. "Didn't you sow good seed in your field?" only leads into their real question, "Where then did the weeds come from?", and the owner answers it. It is not plainly a question asked for force, and the span also starts on a stray comma.

"You of little faith ... why did you doubt?" is a rebuke, not a request for a reason, and Peter gives no answer. The span took in the narrative about Jesus reaching out His hand, so it is cut to the question.

"And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?" throws the Pharisees' question back at them as a charge, and 15:4-6 proves it. The narrative words "Jesus replied," are removed from the span.

Jesus is "aware of their conversation", so "why are you debating among yourselves about having no bread?" is a rebuke and not a request for information. 16:9 follows it with more rebuking questions. The narrative lead-in is removed from the span.
"What do you think, Simon?" really asks for Peter's view, and Peter answers in 17:26 ("From others"). It is not a question that tells. The span also leaves out "What".

The marked "do you think?" is a broken piece of the opening formula. But the verse plainly holds a question that tells: "will he not leave the ninety-nine ... and go out to search for the one that is lost?" (Greek ouchi) expects a yes, and Jesus goes on without waiting for an answer (18:13), just as in 12:11. The span is moved to that question.

"Why do you ask Me about what is good?" is a pointed counter-question. Jesus does not wait for the man's reason and goes straight on. The second span, "There is only One who is good.", is a statement and not part of the question, so it is dropped.

The astonished disciples' "Who then can be saved?" may be a real cry of perplexity, and Jesus answers it in 19:26. It is not plainly a question that tells, and when in doubt the place does not go live.
"Did you not agree with me on one denarius?" reminds the worker of something both of them know, and it proves "I am not being unfair to you." The span started on a stray period, which is trimmed.
"But what do you think?" introduces the parable of the two sons and asks for a judgment that the hearers later give (21:31). It is not a question that tells, and the span also leaves out "what".

The verse says Jesus already "knew their evil intent", so "You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?" is a rebuke and not a request for information. He moves straight on to "Show Me the coin". The narrative lead-in is removed from the span.
"What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is He?" is a real question, and the Pharisees answer it ("David's"). The question that tells comes later, in 22:43-45. The span also leaves out "What".

"Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?" is a reproach to the sleeping disciples and gets no answer. The span started on a stray period and an opening quotation mark, which are trimmed.
The high priest's "What do you think?" calls for a verdict, and the council gives one ("He deserves to die"). It is a real question, not one that tells, and the span also leaves out "What".

"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" is a cry of anguish to God from the cross. The verse does not plainly show it is asked only to make a point and not as a real lament, so in doubt it stays out.

Woken in the storm, the disciples' "don't You care that we are perishing?" is plainly a frightened complaint, not a request for information. The span began with a stray comma left from "Teacher" and now starts at "don't".

Just after the calm, "Why are you so afraid?" and "Do you still have no faith?" are plainly a rebuke. The single span also took in the narration "He asked.", so each question is now marked on its own.
"Overwhelmed with fear", the disciples ask one another "Who is this...?" It reads as real, awed wondering about who He is. It is not plainly a question asked only to make a point.

"And how can He perform such miracles?" comes from people who "were astonished". On its own it may be real puzzlement. The scorn only shows in 6:3 ("Isn't this the carpenter...?", "they took offense"), so in doubt this one stays out.
"Are you still so dull?" and "Do you not understand?" are plainly a reproach, not requests for information. The span began with a stray ". " from "He asked." and now marks the two questions.

"Jesus sighed deeply in His spirit" and then asks "Why does this generation demand a sign?" This is plainly a rebuke, not a request for a reason. The second span, "no sign will be given", is a plain statement that carries no question, so it is removed.
"Do you still not see or understand? Do you have such hard hearts?" are plainly reproaches. The span began with the stray "? " of the question before it. It now marks these two questions.
"Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?" is plainly a reproach. The span ", do you not see?" cut off "Having eyes" and kept a stray comma. It now marks both whole questions.

"Who then can be saved?" carries dismay, but Jesus answers it as a real question in 10:27 ("With man this is impossible, but not with God"). It is not plainly a question that is not asking. The readers split, so in doubt it stays out.
"Jesus saw through their hypocrisy", so "Why are you testing Me?" is plainly a rebuke, not a request for their motive. The span took in the narration and now marks only the question.

"Have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses...?" is put to men who knew the book, and it leads to "You are badly mistaken!" (12:27). It plainly makes a point. The span began with a stray comma and now starts at "have".
"Leave her alone; why are you bothering her?" is plainly a rebuke to those who "scolded her" (14:5). The span took in "But Jesus said, 'Leave her alone;" and now marks only the question.
Jesus "found them sleeping", so "Were you not able to keep watch for one hour?" is plainly a reproach. The span began with a stray ". " from "He asked." and now marks only the question.

"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" is a cry of anguish from the cross. Nothing in the verse plainly shows it is asked only to make a point rather than as a true lament. Same judgment as Matthew 27:46.

"Child, why have You done this to us?" carries reproach, but it is also a real question from anxious parents, and Jesus gives a reason in reply (2:49). It is not plainly a question that is not asking.

"Did you not know that I had to be in My Father's house?" plainly implies that they should have known, so it is not a request for information. The span began with a stray ". " from "He asked." and now marks only the question.

In Nazareth the townspeople know Joseph's son, and the Greek 'ouchi' expects a yes, so 'Isn't this the son of Joseph?' voices wonder, not a request for facts. The span began with the stray period and quote mark from 'lips.' and is trimmed to the question.

The verse says Jesus already knew what they were thinking, so 'Why are you thinking these things in your hearts?' is a rebuke, not a request for facts. The span took in the narrative and is trimmed to the question.

The verse itself says the Pharisees 'complained', so 'Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?' is a reproach in question form. The span took in the narrative and is trimmed to the question.

'Can a blind man lead a blind man?' plainly expects a no, and 'Will they not both fall into a pit?' plainly expects a yes. Neither asks for information. The span began with the stray colon and quote mark, so both questions are marked instead.

The guests say 'Who is this who even forgives sins?' to themselves. It can be read as offence, but just as well as real wonder about who Jesus is (compare 8:25). The verse does not settle which, so it is not plain enough to go live unnamed.

Jesus asks for the lawyer's judgment and gets an answer in 10:37 ('The one who showed him mercy'). That makes it a real, leading question, not plainly one that does not ask. The span also cut off 'Which of these three'.

Martha knows the answer to her own question. 'Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?' is a complaint, and 'Tell her to help me!' follows it at once. The span began with a stray comma and is set to the whole question, 'Lord,' included.
'Did not the One who made the outside make the inside as well?' expects a plain yes and comes right after 'You fools!' as a rebuke. The span began with the stray '!' and is trimmed to the question.

'Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?' means no one did. It turns down the request in 12:13 and asks for no answer. The span began with a stray comma and is set to the whole question, 'Man,' included.

After 'You hypocrites!', 'Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey...?' expects a yes and rebukes them. It asks for no facts. The span began with the stray period and quote mark and is trimmed to the question.

'So if you have not been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches?' plainly means no one will. The span began with a stray comma and left out the 'if' clause the question rests on, so the whole sentence is marked.

'And if you have not been faithful with the belongings of another, who will give you belongings of your own?' plainly means no one will. The span began with a stray comma and left out the 'if' clause, so the whole sentence is marked.

"When the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?" closes the parable as a searching warning. Nobody answers it, and it seeks no information. The marked words, though, took in the statement "I tell you, He will promptly carry out justice on their behalf", so they are cut to the question alone.

"Those who heard this asked, 'Who then can be saved?'" reads as a real question put to Jesus, and He answers it in 18:27 ("What is impossible with man is possible with God"). It is not plainly a question that tells.

Jesus answers His own question with "Is it not the one who reclines?", which expects yes, and then turns it: "But I am among you as one who serves." The figure is plain. The marked words began with a stray "? " left from the sentence before.
The criminal "heaped abuse on Him". "Are You not the Christ?" is a taunt, not an inquiry, so the figure is plain. The marked words began with a stray ". " and an opening quotation mark.

"You are Israel's teacher ... and you do not understand these things?" is plainly a rebuke, not a request. Jesus goes straight on with "Truly, truly, I tell you" and waits for no answer. The marked words were cut off at the apostrophe, so they become the question's two parts on either side of "said Jesus".

"How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?" voices surprise. It can still fairly be read as a real question about why He asks her, and Jesus answers her in 4:10. Since we are in doubt, it is not plain enough to go live.

"So the disciples asked one another, 'Could someone have brought Him food?'" is a real, puzzled question after "I have food to eat that you know nothing about", and Jesus explains in 4:34. It makes no point of its own.
"Woman, where are your accusers?" draws a real answer from her, "No one, Lord" (8:11), and leads on to "neither do I condemn you". It works as dialogue, so it is not plainly a question that tells.
The neighbors really were asking who he was. In 9:9 they are unsure: "Some claimed that he was, but others said, 'No, he just looks like him.'" It is a real question, not a figure.

"Why do you want to hear it again?" comes right after "I already told you, and you did not listen", so it is a protest, not a request for their reason. The marked words are cut to the question alone and leave out the narration and the statement.

"Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?" plainly expects no and backs up "These are not the words of a man possessed by a demon." The marked words drop the stray ". " left over from the sentence before.
The people were "asking one another", "What do you think? Will He come to the feast at all?" These are real questions seeking opinions, not a figure. The marked words also cut off "What".
Thomas's "how can we know the way?" comes from real confusion, and Jesus answers it in 14:6 ("I am the way"). It can be read as a real request, so the figure is not plain.

"Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?" plainly means "I shall" and gives the reason for "Put your sword back in its sheath!" The marked words drop the stray ". " and the opening quote mark.

"Why are you asking Me?" is a protest: He had "spoken openly to the world" (18:20), and "Surely they know what I said." The marked words are cut to the question and leave out the separate command "Ask those who heard My message."

"But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?" shows that the blow had no reason; it does not ask for one. The marked words are cut to that sentence and leave out "Jesus replied" and the first sentence.

"Didn't I see you with Him in the garden?" is an accusing question that waits for an answer, and Peter gives one by denying it (18:27), as with the question in 18:25. It is not plainly a question that asks nothing.
"Do You not know that I have authority to release You and authority to crucify You?" asserts Pilate's power and does not inquire. The marked words drop the stray "? " from the question before.

"why do you stand here looking into the sky?" is a gentle rebuke that moves the disciples on, followed by the promise that He will come back. It does not ask for their reason. The marked words leave out the address and the speech tag.

"why are you surprised by this? Why do you stare at us as if by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk?" are plainly reproofs and a denial that the power was theirs, leading into 3:13. The marked words leave out the narration and take in both questions.

After "Men, you are brothers", "Why are you mistreating each other?" urges them to stop, since Moses "tried to reconcile them". It seeks no reason. The marked words are cut from the whole verse to the question.

After "Heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool", the question means no house can hold Him, as 7:48 says. The question starts at BSB line 3, so the marked words now cover lines 3 and 4, not line 4 alone.

"Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?" is the Lord's rebuke, not a request for Saul's reasons; Saul answers only "Who are You, Lord?" The marked words are cut to the question and leave out the narration.
John asks "Who do you suppose I am?" and answers it himself at once ("I am not that One"), so it seeks no opinion. The marked words put back the missing "Who".
"doesn't everyone know ...?" states what everyone already knows, and 19:36 goes on "Since these things are undeniable". The marked words drop the stray ", " after "Men of Ephesus".

"Why are you weeping and breaking my heart?" protests at their pleading (21:12) and is followed by "I am ready ... to die". It does not ask for a cause. The marked words leave out "Then Paul answered".

"Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?" is the Lord's rebuke, not a request for reasons; Saul answers only "Who are You, Lord?" (22:8). The marked words are cut to the question and leave out the narration.

"Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?" is a rebuke, not a request for reasons, and Saul replies only "Who are You, Lord?". The marked words also took in the narrative "We all fell to the ground...", so they are cut to the question.

"do you think you will escape God's judgment?" plainly means you will not, and the BSB span is right. The tags are the verse's first eight Greek words (the address "O man, you who judge") and miss σὺ ἐκφεύξῃ τὸ κρίμα τοῦ θεοῦ, the words of the question.

"Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness...?" accuses rather than asks, and the BSB shows it plainly, so the flag that it shows only in the original is wrong. The tags cover the noun phrase and miss καταφρονεῖς, the verb the question turns on.

"you, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself?" is plainly a charge. The marked words began with a stray comma, so they now start at "you, then". The tags ὁ οὖν διδάσκων ἕτερον σεαυτὸν οὐ διδάσκεις are exactly that question.

"You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?" is plainly an accusation, and the BSB shows it, so the original-only flag is wrong. The tags stop before τὸν θεὸν ἀτιμάζεις, the verb that carries the question.
"will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?" plainly expects yes. The marked words began with a stray comma. The tags fall on the if-clause, not on οὐχ ... λογισθήσεται.

"What, then, is the advantage of being a Jew?" is raised to be answered at once ("Much in every way", 3:2). The point is made by the answer, and the answer the question seems to suggest (none) is the opposite of Paul's, so it is not plainly a question that tells.

"That God is unjust to inflict His wrath on us?" voices an objection that 3:6 answers ("Certainly not!"). That is question and answer, and so in doubt as a question that tells. The span is also the whole verse, and the tags sit on the if-clause.
"how could God judge the world?" plainly assumes that God will judge the world, and the span is right. The tags include μὴ γένοιτο ("Certainly not!"), which is outside the question, and miss κόσμον.

"why am I still condemned as a sinner?" is a protest meaning "I should not be", not a request for information, and the span is the question. The tags fall on the if-clause, not on τί ἔτι κἀγὼ ὡς ἁμαρτωλὸς κρίνομαι.

"Why not say ... 'Let us do evil that good may result'?" pushes the objection to an absurd end, and "Their condemnation is deserved!" shows no answer is sought. The tags cover καὶ μὴ and the aside, and miss ποιήσωμεν τὰ κακὰ ἵνα ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀγαθά.
"What then? Are we any better? Not at all." is question and answer, and the point is in the answer. The span runs through the whole verse, and the tags mark only Τί οὖν.

"Is God the God of Jews only? Is He not the God of Gentiles too?" is plainly rhetorical, since "only" and "not" give the answer. In Greek it is one question (ἢ Ἰουδαίων ὁ θεὸς μόνον, οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ ἐθνῶν;), so the span now covers both parts. The tags cover all of it except the last word.

"Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith? Certainly not!" raises an objection in order to answer it, and the point is in the answer. The span also takes in "Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law."
"What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather, has discovered?" opens a question that 4:2-3 answer. It makes no point of its own.
"For what does the Scripture say?" only introduces the quotation that answers it, and the span also takes in that quotation.

"Is this blessing only on the circumcised, or also on the uncircumcised?" is an open question that Paul works out in 4:10-12, not one whose answer is plain from the question. The span also takes in the next sentence.
"Was it after his circumcision, or before? It was not after, but before." is question and answer in one verse, so the point is in the answer, and the span includes that answer.

"Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase?" voices an objection that 6:2 answers ("Certainly not!"). That is question and answer, and so in doubt as a question that tells. The tags mark only the formula Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν.

"How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?" plainly means we cannot, and the span is right. The tags include μὴ γένοιτο ("Certainly not!"), which is outside the question, and miss ζήσομεν ἐν αὐτῇ.

"Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under grace? Certainly not!" is an objection answered at once, so the point is in the answer. The marked words begin with a stray "?", and the tags mark only Τί οὖν, which lies outside the marked words.

"What fruit did you reap ... from the things of which you are now ashamed?" plainly implies no fruit worth having. The span is cut to the question, without the statement "The outcome of those things is death." The tags miss ἐπαισχύνεσθε, and the original-only flag is wrong because the BSB shows the figure.
"What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not!" is objection and answer, so the point is in the answer. The marked words are the whole verse, and the tags mark only Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν.
"Did that which is good, then, become death to me? Certainly not!" raises an objection in order to answer it, and the point is in the answer. The span also runs through the whole answer.
"Who hopes for what he can already see?" plainly means no one does. The span is cut to the question, and the tags sit on the statements before it, not on τίς, τί καὶ ἐλπίζει.

"how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?" plainly means that He will, and the marked words are the question itself. The tags fall on the premise (ὅς γε τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ οὐκ ἐφείσατο, ἀλλ᾽) and on τὰ, not on πῶς οὐχὶ ... χαρίσεται, so they are stripped.

"Is God unjust? Certainly not!" raises an objection and then answers it. The point is made by "Certainly not!", not by the question, so this is question-and-answer, which is not a live form, and not a question that tells on its own. Doubt means drop. The marked words also begin with a stray "? ", and the tags mark Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν, which is outside the marked words.

"For who can resist His will?" plainly makes the objector's point that no one can, and "who can resist His will?" is an exact part of the verse. The tags cover Ἐρεῖς μοι οὖν· τί οὖν ἔτι μέμφεται and only τίς of the marked question, missing τῷ βουλήματι αὐτοῦ ... ἀνθέστηκεν, so they are stripped.

This verse is the middle of one unfinished sentence that runs from 9:22 to 9:24. The BSB supplies "What if", and the verse ends in a dash. In the Greek, καὶ ἵνα γνωρίσῃ is a purpose clause with no question word, so the claim that the figure shows only in the original is backwards. The figure is not plain at these words, and the tags are just the first eight words.

"What then will we say?" only leads into Paul's own conclusion, which he then states outright ("That the Gentiles ... have obtained it"). It is a question answered at once, not a question that tells, and the marked words take in the answer as well. No live form fits.
"Why not?" only sets up Paul's own answer ("Because their pursuit was not by faith"). The question itself tells nothing, so the figure is not plain.
"'Who will descend into the Abyss?'" is a question Paul tells the reader not to say in his heart. Whether it is a real question or one that tells needs interpreting, so it is not plain.
"But what does it say?" only leads into the quotation that answers it and makes no point of its own. The marked words also take in the whole verse.

"Lord, who has believed our message?" plainly means few have, as "not all of them welcomed the good news" shows. The span started with a stray comma and dropped "Lord". The tags fall on the statement "But not all heeded the good news; Isaiah for", not on the question.
"did God reject His people?" uses Greek me, which expects no, and "Certainly not!" follows. The span was a fragment that started with a comma. The tags are on the question's words.

"Do you not know what the Scripture says about Elijah..." plainly expects yes. The span took in the statement "God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew", and the tags fall on that statement, not on the question.
"And what was the divine reply to him?" only leads into the quoted answer and makes no point of its own. The marked words also take in the whole answer.
"What then?" is a bare link to the next point, which Paul gives at once. The question tells nothing, and the span covers the whole verse.

"did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery?" is a me-question that expects no, followed by "Certainly not!". The span took in the whole verse, statement included. The tags are on the question sentence.

The BSB has an exclamation, "how much greater riches will their fullness bring!", not a question. The Greek question mark was added by an editor to a how-much-more argument, so the figure is not plain. The tags fall on the if-clause.

"what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?" plainly states its answer as a question, and the BSB shows it. The question is the main clause, not the if-clause. The tags fall mostly on the if-clause (ei gar he apobole auton katallage kosmou).

The BSB ends with an exclamation, "how much more readily will these... be grafted into their own olive tree!". It is an argument from the lesser to the greater, and the Greek question mark is an editor's. The tags fall on the if-clause.

"Do you want to be unafraid of the one in authority? Then do what is right" uses the question as an if-clause, and the command answers it. It is not plainly a question that tells. The tags fall on "For rulers are not a terror to good conduct".

"For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him?" plainly means no one does, as the next sentence confirms. The span also took in that statement. The tags are on the question's words.

"are you not worldly? Are you not walking in the way of man?" are ouchi-questions that plainly expect yes. The span was a fragment that started with a comma. The tags fall on "for you are still worldly" and "since... among you", not on ouchi sarkikoi este.
"are you not mere men?" plainly expects yes. The when-clause only sets the scene, so the question is the figure. The tags cover the when-clause and leave out ouk anthropoi.

"What then is Apollos? And what is Paul?" are questions Paul answers at once ("They are servants..."). The answer makes the point, not the question, so the figure is not plain. The span also takes in the answer.

"Shouldn't you rather have been stricken with grief...?" is plainly a rebuke. The span started with the stray "!" of "And you are proud!". Half the tags fall on that statement (kai humeis pephusiomenoi este).
"Do you not know that a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough?" plainly expects yes. The span started with a stray period. The first tags fall on "Your boasting is not good".

Both questions plainly tell: "What business of mine..." means it is none, and "Are you not to judge those inside?" expects yes. The span started with a stray "?". The tags are on the first question, so both questions are marked.

The BSB has no question here. "how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints!" is plainly an indignant outburst, so it is kept as an exclamation and the if-clause is left out. The Greek question mark is an editor's. The tags fall on "a matter having against the other".

"Is there really no one among you wise enough...?" is plainly a question meant to shame. The span also took in the statement "I say this to your shame", and half the tags fall on it (pros entropen humin lego).

"Why not rather be wronged?" plainly urges and does not ask for reasons, and the span is right. The tags fall on the statement before it (ede men oun holos hettema en humin estin), not on dia ti ouchi mallon adikeisthe.

"Was a man already circumcised when he was called?" stands for "if a man was", and a command answers it. It states a case and is not plainly a question that tells. The span also takes in the commands.

"Were you a slave when you were called?" stands for "if you were a slave", and the instruction answers it. It states a case and is not plainly a question that tells. The span also takes in the instruction.

"Are you committed to a wife?" works as an "if" (if you are bound, do not seek release). It does not make a point the way a question that tells does. The span also takes in both commands, and the tags miss λέλυσαι.
"will he not be encouraged...?" plainly expects yes. I dropped the stray leading comma. The tags sit on the if-clause (ἐὰν γάρ τις ἴδῃ σὲ...), not on οὐχὶ ... οἰκοδομηθήσεται.

Both questions plainly tell: the first expects no and the second expects yes. The old span began with a stray "?" and left out the first question. The tags cover only the first question (and a stray ταῦτα), so they do not match the figure.

"Is it about oxen that God is concerned?" plainly expects no, and 9:10 answers it. The span should be the question, not the Law quotation. The tags sit on the quotation (ἐν γὰρ τῷ Μωϋσέως νόμῳ γέγραπται· οὐ κημώσεις).
The whole verse is one question, and it plainly means "it is not too much". The tags mark the if-clause and the repeated pronouns but miss σαρκικὰ θερίσομεν, so they do not point at the figure.
"shouldn't we have it all the more?" plainly expects yes. I dropped the stray leading comma. The tags fall mostly on the if-clause and spill into the next sentence (οὐκ, τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ).
Paul asks "What then is my reward?" only to give his own answer, not to learn anything. The span should be the question alone, not the answer. The tags τίς οὖν μού ἐστιν ὁ μισθός are the question.
"Are not those who eat the sacrifices...?" plainly expects yes. I dropped the stray leading colon. The tags fall mostly on the command βλέπετε τὸν Ἰσραὴλ κατὰ σάρκα and the name, not the question.

"why should my freedom be determined by someone else's conscience?" makes a point, not a request for information, and the span is right. The tags sit on the earlier clause (συνείδησιν δὲ λέγω οὐχὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ...), not on ἱνατί ... κρίνεται.
"why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?" plainly protests rather than asks, and the span is right. Five of the eight tags are on the if-clause εἰ δὲ ἐγὼ χάριτι μετέχω.

The question plainly expects no; 11:14 goes on with "Doesn't nature itself teach you". The span should leave out the command "Judge for yourselves:". The tags start on that command (ἐν ὑμῖν αὐτοῖς κρίνατε) and miss τῷ θεῷ προσεύχεσθαι.

The question opens in 11:14 ("Doesn't nature itself teach you..."). This verse holds only its tail plus a plain statement, "For long hair is given to her as a covering", so the figure is not at these words.

The BSB has no question here ("that would not make it any less a part of the body"); the question exists only in editors' Greek punctuation. But the foot plainly speaks as a person, so it is kept as a thing spoken of as a person, marking the foot's words. The tags also mark the final clause, so they are dropped.
places.words_why: A foot is plainly made to speak: "If the foot should say, 'Because I am not a hand...'". The words that carry the figure are "the foot should say". The quoted speech only follows from it.

places.why: As in 12:15, the BSB reads a statement, not a question. The ear plainly speaks as a person, so it is kept as a thing spoken of as a person, marking its words. The tags spill into the final clause and miss ὀφθαλμός and σώματος.
places.words_why: The ear is plainly made to speak: "And if the ear should say, 'Because I am not an eye...'". The words that carry the figure are "the ear should say".

places.why: Both questions plainly show the absurdity in question form, so the second, parallel question is now marked too. Most tags sit on the if-clauses (εἰ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα ὀφθαλμός).
"where would the body be?" plainly answers itself (there would be none), and the span is right. Seven of the eight tags are on the if-clause εἰ δὲ ἦν τὰ πάντα ἓν μέλος, and σῶμα is untagged.

"how will I benefit you, unless...?" plainly means not at all, and the span is right. The tags are on "Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues" (Νῦν δέ ἀδελφοί ἐὰν ἔλθω...), not on τί ὑμᾶς ὠφελήσω.
"how will anyone recognize the tune...?" plainly means no one will, and the span is right. The tags cover the opening (ὅμως τὰ ἄψυχα φωνὴν διδόντα, εἴτε αὐλὸς), not πῶς γνωσθήσεται.
"who will prepare for battle?" plainly means no one. I dropped the stray leading comma. Seven of the eight tags are on the if-clause καὶ γὰρ ἐὰν ἄδηλον σάλπιγξ φωνὴν δῷ.

"how will anyone know what you are saying?" plainly means no one will, and "You will just be speaking into the air" follows. The span is right. The tags are on οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς διὰ τῆς γλώσσης ἐὰν μὴ, not πῶς γνωσθήσεται.
Paul asks "What then shall I do?" only to give his own answer. The span should be the question alone, not the answer that follows. The tags τί οὖν ἐστιν are right.
"how can someone who is uninstructed say 'Amen'...?" plainly means he cannot, and the span is right. The tags are on ἐπεὶ ἐὰν εὐλογῇς ἐν πνεύματι and articles, not on πῶς ἐρεῖ.
"will they not say that you are out of your minds?" plainly expects yes. I dropped the stray leading comma. All the tags are on the if-clause ἐὰν οὖν συνέλθῃ ἡ ἐκκλησία ὅλη ἐπὶ τὸ.

Paul asks "What then shall we say, brothers?" and answers it himself at once. The span should be the question alone, not the answer through "to build up the church". The tags Τί οὖν ἐστιν, ἀδελφοί are right.

"how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?" plainly challenges rather than asks, and the span is right. The tags are on the if-clause Εἰ δὲ Χριστὸς κηρύσσεται..., and πῶς λέγουσιν is untagged.

"what did I gain?" plainly means "nothing" if the dead are not raised. It makes a point and asks for no answer, and the marked words are the question itself. The tags do not fit the figure. Six of the eight sit on the if-clause εἰ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον ἐθηριομάχησα ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, the place name among them, a seventh is on the next "if" (εἰ before νεκροὶ), and ὄφελος, the word that carries the question, is untagged.

These are questions Paul puts in an objector's mouth so that he can answer them at length (15:36 onward). Paul treats them as real questions, so the verse does not plainly show questions that are not asking, and when in doubt a place does not go live. The marked words and tags also take in "But someone will ask" (Ἀλλ᾽ ἐρεῖ τις), which is not part of any question.

"who is left to cheer me but those whom I have grieved?" plainly means "no one but you". It makes a point rather than asking. The words that carry the figure are the question, not the if-clause "For if I grieve you,", so I narrowed the marked words to match 1 Corinthians 15:32, where only the question is marked. The tags do not fit. Five of the eight are on εἰ γὰρ ἐγὼ λυπῶ ὑμᾶς, the ninth is the "except" εἰ, and ὁ εὐφραίνων με is untagged.

"And who is qualified for such a task?" plainly makes a point rather than asks (3:5 answers it). The marked words should be the question alone, not the statement before it. The tags sit on the odor/death words, not on τίς ἱκανός.

"What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols?" plainly means "none", and the marked words are that question. The tag numbers also light ναὸς θεοῦ and θεὸς twice in "we are the temple of the living God" and "I will be their God", outside the question, so the Greek marks would mislead.

In the BSB there is no question here. "what earnestness, what eagerness ... what vindication!" is a plain exclamation, so the place stays under that form, marked at the exclamation only and without the statement after it. The tags sit on ἰδοὺ γὰρ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ... λυπηθῆναι, not on the exclamation.

"Why? Because I do not love you?" is raised only to be denied at once. The marked words should end at the questions, not take in the answer "God knows I do!". The tags (διὰ τί) are on the question's own words.

"Are they servants of Christ?" is plainly rhetorical, like the questions in 11:22. The marked words should be that question, not the list of labors after it. The tags (διάκονοι Χριστοῦ εἰσιν) are exactly right.

The questions are plainly not asking, but the tags (G5101, G0770G, G2532, G3756, G0770G) are exactly the five words of the first question, "Who is weak, and I am not weak?". The marked English also takes in "Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with grief?", whose own words (G4624, G1473, G4448) are untagged, and "and" is tagged twice. The tags do not match the marked words.
A plainly ironic question, followed by "Forgive me this wrong!". The marked words left out the opening "In". The tags are on the question's own words; the only stray mark is one article.

Both questions are plainly rhetorical, expecting "no" and then "yes". The marked words began with a stray "?" and left out the first question. The tags take in the statement "I urged Titus ... sent our brother".

"Can't you see for yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you?" plainly expects "yes". The marked words began with a stray ".". The tags sit on the commands "Examine yourselves ... test yourselves", not on ἢ οὐκ ἐπιγινώσκετε.

"Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God?" is answered by Paul himself in the same verse, and the marked words are right. The tag numbers also light γὰρ and ἀνθρώποις twice in the later clauses ("If I were still trying to please men"), outside the marked question.

"how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?" is plainly a rebuke, and the marked words are right. The tags are on the narrative "When I saw that they were not walking in line ...", not on πῶς ... ἀναγκάζεις.

The question is plainly raised only to be rejected by "Certainly not!". The marked words should be the question, not the answer or the whole if-clause. The tags fall on the if-clause and miss ἆρα ... ἁμαρτίας διάκονος.

"Who has bewitched you?" is a plain rebuke, not a request for a name. The marked words began with a stray "!". The tags also cover Ὦ ἀνόητοι Γαλάται and τῇ ἀληθείᾳ, which are outside the marked question.

Paul plainly already knows the answer. The marked words should be the question, not the lead-in "I would like to learn just one thing from you". The tags sit mostly on that lead-in, not on τὸ πνεῦμα ἐλάβετε.

"Why then was the law given?" is raised only so that Paul can answer it. The marked words should be the question alone, not the answer after it. The tags (Τί οὖν ὁ νόμος) are the question's words; the only stray marks are two articles.

The question is plainly raised only to be rejected ("Certainly not!"). The marked words should be the question alone. The tag numbers also light νόμος, νόμου and articles in the later sentence "For if a law had been given ...".

"What then has become of your blessing?" is a plain lament, not an inquiry. The marked words should be the question, not the next sentence. The tags (Ποῦ οὖν ἦν ὁ μακαρισμὸς ὑμῶν) are right; the stray marks are only pronouns and an article.
A plain challenge that 4:22 goes on to answer. The marked words began with a stray comma. The tags sit on "Tell me, you who want to be under the law" and miss οὐκ ἀκούετε.

"But what does the Scripture say?" asks nothing; it brings in the quotation that answers it. The marked words should be the question, not the quotation. The tags (ἀλλὰ τί λέγει ἡ γραφή) are right; the other marks are only articles.

"why am I still being persecuted?" plainly argues that he is not preaching circumcision, and the marked words are right. The tags are mostly on the if-clause (Ἐγὼ δέ ἀδελφοί εἰ περιτομὴν ἔτι κηρύσσω) and miss διώκομαι.
"What then is the issue?" is asked only so that Paul can answer it at once with "Just this". The marked words should be the question, not the whole verse. The tags (τί γάρ) are exactly right.

The verse is a single reproving question: "If you have died with Christ ..., why ... do you submit to its regulations". The marked words are right. The tags all fall on the if-clause, and τί ... δογματίζεσθε is not tagged.
"how can he care for the church of God?" plainly means he cannot, and the marked words are right. The tags are on the if-clause, not on πῶς ... ἐπιμελήσεται.
The BSB verse is a statement with no question in it. The only sign of one is an editors' question mark in the Greek, and no other form shows plainly at the marked words.
"how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?" plainly means "we shall not", and the marked words are right. The tags are on πῶς ... σωτηρίας; the only stray mark is the pronoun ἡμᾶς.

Both questions are plainly rhetorical: the writer answers the first with the second. The marked words began with a stray "?" and left out the first question. Once that question is marked, the tags (τίνες γὰρ ἀκούσαντες παρεπίκραναν) point at it.

"Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?" plainly expects the answer yes. It is a question asked to make a point, the same pattern as 3:16 and 3:18. The marked words started with a stray "?", so they are now just that question, copied from the BSB. The Strong's tags were on the earlier question (τίσιν δὲ προσώχθισεν τεσσεράκοντα ἔτη), not on the οὐχὶ question that carries the figure, so they are stripped.

"Was it not to those who disobeyed?" expects yes and makes the point. The marked words start with the "?" left over from the first question, so they are trimmed to the question itself. The tags sit on the first question (tisin ... katapausin) and miss apeithesasin, so they do not point at the figure.

"why was there still need for another priest to appear...?" plainly means there was no need. The BSB shows the question, so the note "shows only in the original" is wrong. The tags light the if-clause and scattered articles and miss the question words tis eti chreia.
The BSB gives an exclamation ending in "!", not a question. The question rests only on the editors' ";" in the Greek, so the figure is not plain to a reader of the BSB. When in doubt, it stays out.
"would not the offerings have ceased?" expects yes, and the writer goes straight on to argue it. The marked words start with a stray comma, so they become the whole question sentence.

"what more shall I say?" is answered by "Time will not allow me to tell", so it is plainly not asking. The marked words are right. The app lights every word of each tagged root, so the G2532 tag would also light the four kai in the list of names, which are not part of the question.

"For what son is not disciplined by his father?" plainly means every son is. The marked words took in the commands before it, so they are trimmed to the question. The BSB shows it, so the "only in the original" note is wrong. The tags light the commands and miss tis ... ou paideuei.

"Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live?" expects yes. The marked words start with the period from the sentence before, so they are trimmed. The tags light the earthly-fathers statement and miss ou polu de mallon hupotagesometha.

"What can man do to me?" plainly means nothing, and the marked words are the BSB's own poetry line 3. The tags light "So we say with confidence: The Lord is my helper; and" and miss ti poiesei ... anthropos.

"Has not God chosen the poor of this world...?" expects yes. The marked words start with the colon after the address, so they are trimmed. The tags light the call "akousate, adelphoi mou agapetoi", which is outside the question, and scattered articles.

"Is it not the rich who oppress you...?" expects yes. The marked words start with the period from the statement before, so they are trimmed. Five tags light that statement (humeis de etimasate ton ptochon), which is outside the question.

"what good is that?" plainly means no good at all. The marked words began in the middle of the if-clause, so they become the question itself. The tags light "may say ... go in" and miss ti to ophelos.
The BSB reads "You see that his faith was working with his actions...", a plain statement. The question rests only on the editors' ";" in the Greek, so the figure is not plain.

"was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions...?" expects yes. The marked words started with a stray comma and cut off "In the same way", so they become the whole question, which is the whole verse. The tags, including ouk, all lie inside the Greek question.

"can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs?" expects no, and the verse says so next. The marked words start with a stray comma, so they are trimmed. The app lights every word of each tagged root, so G4160 would also light poiesai in the next statement, and ampelos suka are untagged.

"Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it..." uses the question as a way of saying "whoever is wise" to lead into a command. It does not plainly make a point of its own, so it stays out.

"Don't they come from the passions at war within you?" expects yes and answers the first question. The marked words start with the "?" of the first question, so they are trimmed. The tags light the first question and miss ouk enteuthen.

"Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?" expects yes and rebukes. The marked words start with the "!" of "You adulteresses!", so they are trimmed. The tags light the address moichoi kai moichalides and articles in the next statement.

"who are you to judge your neighbor?" is a rebuke, not a request to learn. The marked words are right. The tags light the statement before it (heis estin ho nomothetes kai krites ho dunamenos) and miss su de tis ... krinon.

"Is any one of you suffering? He should pray." uses the question to mean "if anyone is suffering" and introduces an instruction, so it is not plainly a question that makes a point. The marked words also take in the commands.
As in 5:13, "Is any one of you sick?" stands for "if anyone is sick" and introduces an instruction, so it is not plainly a question that tells. The marked words also cover the whole command.

"How is it to your credit if you are beaten for doing wrong...?" plainly means it is no credit. The marked words ran into the next statement, so they are trimmed to the question. The BSB shows it, so the "only in the original" note is wrong. The app lights every word of each tagged root, so ei, kai and hupomeneite in the next statement would light too.

"what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God?" plainly implies a terrible end. The marked words took in the statement before it, so they are trimmed. The note "only in the original" is wrong. The tags light the statement (hoti ho kairos ... apo) and miss ti to telos.

"If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?" plainly implies ruin, and the BSB shows it. The marked words drop the joining "And," of poetry line 1. The tags light "And" and the if-clause and miss the question words pou phaneitai.

The scoffers' "Where is the promise of His coming?" plainly mocks, as v. 3 and "everything continues as it has" show. The marked words are right. The tags also light kai legontes ("they will ask") and hoi in the next sentence, which are outside the question.

"Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies...?" answers itself, and the BSB shows it, so the "only in the original" note is wrong. The marked words took in the next statement, so they are trimmed. The app lights every word of each tagged root, so estin, ho and arnoumenos in "This is the antichrist..." would light too.

John asks "And why did Cain slay him?" only so he can answer it himself ("Because his own deeds were evil"). He is not asking for information, and a careful reader sees that in the BSB. The marked span was the whole verse, so it is narrowed to the question. The tags were on "ou kathos Kain ek tou ponerou en kai", not on charin tinos, so they are stripped.

"how can the love of God abide in him?" plainly means it cannot, and the marked words are right. The tags fall on the if-clause (Hos d' an eche ton bion tou kosmou) and on articles, and pos ... menei is untagged, so the tags are stripped.

The question "Who then overcomes the world?" is rhetorical, but the marked words also take in the answer, "Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God." That answer is a plain statement, not part of the question, so the span is wrong. The other places in this batch that ask and answer mark only the question.

"Who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?" is a herald's real summons. 5:3 says no one was found, and 5:5 names the Lamb, so it is not plainly a question asked without seeking an answer. The span and the tags also take in the narrative "And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming in a loud voice".

"How long, O Lord ... until You avenge our blood...?" is a plea that gets a real answer in 6:11 ("rest a little while longer, until..."), so the verse does not plainly show a question that is not asking. When in doubt it does not go live. The tags are mostly on the narrative frame kai ekraxan phone megale legontes.

"who is able to withstand it?" plainly means no one, and the marked words are right. All the tags sit on "For the great day of Their wrath has come" (hoti elthen he hemera ... orges), and none are on tis dunatai stathenai, so they are stripped.

"These in white robes, who are they, and where have they come from?" is a question in a dialogue put to John, who replies "Sir, you know", and the elder then answers in 7:14. It is not plainly a question that only makes a point. The span and the tags also take in the narrative "Then one of the elders addressed me".

"Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?" is the worshipers' acclamation and means no one can, so it plainly does not ask for information. The marked words are right. The Greek tags mark the opening narrative ("they worshiped the dragon who gave authority"), not the question itself, so they come off.

The angel asks "Why are you so amazed?" and does not wait for an answer: he goes straight on with "I will tell you the mystery." So the question is plainly not asking. The marked words are right. The tags also take in "and the angel said to me" and many articles that have nothing to do with the figure, so they come off.

"What city was ever like this great city?" they will exclaim. This plainly says that no city ever was. The marked span began with a stray ". " left over from the sentence before, so it now starts at the quotation. The tags mark "cried out, seeing the smoke of her burning" and not the question, so they come off.

places.words_why: "he slept with Hagar, and she conceived". "Slept with" is the gentle phrase. "Hagar" is only its object, so trim to the phrase.

places.why: The marked BSB words "Sarah had passed the age of childbearing" are a plain statement, not a gentle word. The gentle phrase is only in the Hebrew ("a way like the women"), and a BSB reader would not see a euphemism in the lit words. When in doubt, drop.

places.words_why: "two daughters who have never slept with a man". "Slept with" is the gentle phrase. "a man" is its object.
"there is no man in the land to sleep with us". "Sleep with" is the gentle phrase. "us" is its object.
"so we can sleep with him and preserve his line". "Sleep with" is the gentle phrase. "him" is its object.

places.why: "the firstborn went in and slept with her father" plainly uses a gentle phrase for sexual relations. The old span "slept with her" cut off "father" and misread the verse, so the mark is now just "slept with", the words that carry the figure.
"I slept with my father last night" is plainly a euphemism. The old span "slept with my" ended on a dangling "my", so the mark is now just the figure's words, "slept with".

places.words_why: "the younger daughter went in and slept with him". "Slept with" is the gentle phrase. "him" is its object.

"Now Abimelech had not gone near her". In context ("you are as good as dead because of the woman you have taken"), "gone near" is plainly a gentle phrase for relations. "had not" and "her" sit beside it and are not the figure.

places.why: "I have kept you from sinning against Me. That is why I did not let you touch her": with Abimelech having taken Sarah, "touch" plainly stands for sexual relations. "did not let you" is God holding him back and is not part of the figure, so the mark is now "touch her".
places.words_why: "I have kept you from sinning against Me. That is why I did not let you touch her." In context, "touch" is plainly a gentle word for relations. "her" is only its object.
"a virgin who had not had relations with any man". The gentle phrase is "had relations with". The "had not" before it is not the figure.

places.why: "he breathed his last and died ... and was gathered to his people": the verse already says plainly that he died, so the phrase does not stand in for a hard word. Whether it speaks gently of death, of burial, or of joining the dead takes a commentary to decide, so it is not plain enough to go live.

"Then he breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people": the verse names death outright first, so the phrase does not take the place of a hard word. Calling it a euphemism needs interpretation.
"One of the people could easily have slept with your wife" is plainly a euphemism. The old span "slept with your" ended on a dangling "your", so the mark is now "slept with".

places.words_why: "Grant me my wife, for my time is complete, and I want to sleep with her." "Sleep with" is the gentle phrase. "her" is its object.
"gave her to Jacob, and he slept with her." "Slept with" is the gentle phrase. "her" is its object.
"Jacob slept with Rachel as well". "Slept with" is the gentle phrase. The name "Rachel" is not the figure.
"Here is my maidservant Bilhah. Sleep with her, that she may bear children for me". "Sleep with" is the gentle phrase. "her" is its object.
"So Rachel gave Jacob her servant Bilhah as a wife, and he slept with her". "Slept with" is the gentle phrase. "her" is its object.
"he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son's mandrakes". "Sleep with" is the gentle phrase. "you" is its object.
"So he slept with her that night." "Slept with" is the gentle phrase. "her" is its object.

places.why: In the BSB, "for I am having my period" is just the ordinary plain way to say it, so a reader would not see a gentle word standing in for a hard one. The gentle phrase is only in the Hebrew "[the] way of women", and the BSB words marked to carry it also take in "I am having". Since it is in doubt whether a reader of the marked words would see the figure without being told, it does not go live.

places.words_why: "he took her and lay with her by force". "Lay with" is the gentle phrase for intercourse. "her" is its object.

places.why: "Reuben went in and slept with his father’s concubine Bilhah" is plainly a euphemism. The old span "slept with his" ended on a dangling "his", so the mark is now "slept with".

"Then he breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people": the death is stated outright, so the phrase does not replace a hard word. Reading it as a euphemism rather than as burial or joining the dead takes a commentary.

places.words_why: "he took her as a wife and slept with her": "slept with" carries the gentle word for sexual union; "her" is only the object.

places.why: "Sleep with your brother’s wife ... raise up offspring for your brother" is plainly a euphemism. The old span "Sleep with your" ended on a dangling "your", so the mark is now "Sleep with".
"whenever he would sleep with his brother’s wife" is plainly a euphemism. The old span "sleep with his" ended on a dangling "his", so the mark is now "sleep with".

places.words_why: "let me sleep with you": "sleep with" is the gentle phrase; "you" is only the object.
"slept with her, and she became pregnant by him": "slept with" carries the euphemism; "her" is only the object.
"he did not have relations with her again": "have relations with" is the gentle phrase; "did not" is not part of it.
"cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, 'Sleep with me.'": "Sleep with" is the gentle phrase; "me" is only the object.
"he refused to go to bed with her": "go to bed with" is plainly a gentle phrase for sexual relations; "her" is only the object.
"She grabbed Joseph by his cloak and said, 'Sleep with me!'": "Sleep with" carries the euphemism; "me" is only the object.
"He came to me so he could sleep with me": "sleep with" is the gentle phrase; "me" is only the object.

places.why: "bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow" does not soften anything; it makes Jacob's grief stronger, so it is not a euphemism. But hair cannot go down to Sheol by itself, so "gray hair" plainly stands for the old man himself, a part for the whole. Kept as synecdoche on "gray hair".

The verse has just said plainly "he will die", so "brought the gray hair ... down to Sheol" softens nothing. What it plainly shows is "gray hair" standing for the aged father, a part for the whole. Kept as synecdoche on "gray hair" alone, without "of your servant our father".

"because you went up to your father’s bed, onto my couch, and defiled it" plainly speaks of Reuben's sexual sin in veiled words. The figure is the act of going up to the bed, so the marked words are widened to "went up to your father’s bed" to take in the verb.

The verse already names the death plainly ("breathed his last"), and then "he was gathered to his people" is said beside it, so the phrase does not take the place of a harder word. He is not buried until chapter 50, so it may say more than death. When in doubt, drop.

places.words_why: "seduces a virgin ... and sleeps with her": "sleeps with" is the gentle phrase; "her" is only the object.

places.why: "Whoever lies with an animal" plainly uses "lies with" as a gentle phrase for a sexual act. The span is cut back from "lies with an" to "lies with" so it does not end on a stray article.

places.words_why: "If a man lies with a woman and there is an emission of semen": "lies with" carries the euphemism; "a woman" is only the object.
"If a man lies with her and her menstrual flow touches him": "lies with" is the gentle phrase; "her" is only the object.

places.why: "a man who lies with an unclean woman" plainly uses "lies with" for intercourse. The span is cut back from "lies with an" to "lies with".

places.words_why: "You must not lie with a man as with a woman": "lie with" carries the euphemism; "a man" is only the object.

"Beat your plowshares into swords" is a summons of the nations to the valley of judgment (3:12). Seeing irony depends on the reversed words elsewhere or a commentator's note; it is not plain from the verse.
"Leave Him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to save Him" may be scoffing or may be waiting to see. The verse does not plainly show words meaning their opposite.
The verse says they "mocked Him", but "He saved others" is not words saying the opposite of what they mean; the sneer is a plain taunt, and the irony of its truth is a later reader's insight.

places.words_why: The verse before says they "mocked Him", and in "Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross" the titles are said to mean the opposite: the mockers do not believe He is the Christ. The titles carry the irony. "come down now from the cross" is the taunt, not words that mean their opposite.

places.why: The men "began to mock Him" (22:63) and blindfolded Him: their demand "Prophesy! Who hit You?" plainly means the opposite, that He is no prophet. The marked span began with a stray quotation mark and cut off "You?", so it is replaced with the whole taunt.

The rulers sneer, but the marked "He saved others" does not say the opposite of what is meant; any figure sits in "if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One", and even that is a conditional taunt rather than plain irony.
"save Yourself!" is a taunt, a dare that He cannot do it, not words saying the opposite of what is meant. Irony is not plain in these marked words.
"Save Yourself and us!" is abuse from a criminal who partly wants rescue. The words do not plainly say the opposite of what he means.
Pilate's "Shall I crucify your King?" could be a taunt or a last appeal after he "tried to release Him" (19:12). The verse does not plainly show irony.
"What you are doing is not good" is the ordinary Hebrew way of saying wrong, and 18:18 states the harm plainly. Nothing shows less said than meant.
"On this altar you must not offer unauthorized incense..." is a plain prohibition with no understatement, and the whole verse is marked.
"He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished" is emphatic, not lessened. The doubled Hebrew verb is not shown in the BSB and the place has no tags for it.
"My soul will not despise you" is the literal reverse of the curse "My soul will despise you" (26:30). It may be litotes, but the verse does not plainly say less than it means.
"Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished" quotes Exodus 34:7 and is emphatic, not understated.
"the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished" is a natural negative way of saying He will punish. Saying less to mean more is not plain from the verse.
"where you will lack nothing" states full plenty outright beside "eat food without scarcity". Nothing is lessened.

"This thing you have done is not good" before "all of you deserve to die" might understate, but lo tov is the ordinary idiom for wrong, so it is not plain. The second span "not protect" and its tag on the lo' of "you watched" are a literal charge, not part of any figure.

In the BSB, "What you are doing is not right" reads as a plain rebuke. A reader would not see less said than meant without a commentary. "Shouldn't" opens a question, not an understatement, and its tag on ha.Lo' marks that question.
The BSB reads "the hand of God has struck me", which is not mild wording. Any understatement in a Hebrew "touched" does not show in the BSB, the place has no tags, and the whole verse is marked.
"Be not far from me, for trouble is near" is a plain plea for nearness and help. Nothing is said less than it is meant.

"He has not despised or detested" answers 22:6, where the psalmist is "despised by the people", and the verse goes on "but has attended to his cry for help". It reads as a literal contrast, so the understatement is not plain from the verse.
"Those who fear Him lack nothing" is a full, absolute promise. Nothing is said less than it is meant.
"Lack no good thing" is a complete promise set against "Young lions go lacking". It is a plain contrast, not an understatement.
"Be not silent" is a direct plea for God to act, and 35:23 says outright "Awake and rise". Nothing in it is lessened.

The verse sets "a path that is not good" between "he plots wickedness" and "fails to reject evil", so the reader can see that "not good" means an evil path. The second mark, "he fails", carries no figure and is removed. The tags rightly mark lo' tov.
places.words_why: Between "plots wickedness" and "fails to reject evil", "a path that is not good" plainly means an evil path. The figure is carried by "not good", not by "that is".

places.why: "Be not far from me" is a plain plea that restates line 1, and 38:22 follows with "Come quickly to help me". It is not understatement.
"Be not far from me, O God" is an urgent plea, and line 2 asks for the same thing outright. It is not a lessened statement.
"He will not despise their prayer" restates line 1 in the negative. Nothing in the verse shows it means far more than it says, so understatement is only one possible reading, not a plain one.
"O God of my praise, be not silent" is a direct cry for God to act. It is not understatement.
"Be assured that the wicked will not go unpunished" is an emphatic assurance of punishment. The verse does not show that less is said than meant.
"Be assured that he will not go unpunished" is an emphatic certainty of judgment, not a plain understatement.
The path a "violent man" entices his neighbor into is plainly violence, so the verse itself shows the mild "a path that is not good" understating it, as in Psalm 36:4. The tags rightly mark lo' tov.
places.words_why: A violent man "leads him down a path that is not good": the path is plainly ruinous, and "not good" says less than is meant. Only "not good" carries the figure.

places.why: "Whoever gloats over calamity will not go unpunished" is a plain assurance that punishment will come, not a lessened statement made for force.

The verse itself names a gross injustice, "to punish the innocent or to flog a noble for his honesty", and calls it only "not good", so the understatement is plain. The two marks overlapped, so only "not good" stays. The tags rightly mark lo' tov.
"Even zeal is no good without knowledge" reads naturally as a plain verdict that zeal alone is useless. The understatement is not plain, and the second mark wrongly takes in "without".
"Will not go unpunished ... will not escape" are two parallel assurances of certain judgment, not a plainly lessened statement.
"Will not go unpunished" reads as a firm assurance, with line 2 going on to "will perish". The verse does not plainly show an understatement.

places.words_why: The first line calls unequal weights "detestable to the LORD", so "dishonest scales are no good" plainly understates. The figure is "no good", without the verb "are".

places.why: Within this verse, "To show partiality in judgment is not good" reads as the proverb's plain verdict. Only the next verse shows how grave the wrong is, so the figure is not plain in the verse itself. In doubt, it stays out.
"It is not good to eat too much honey" is mild, literal advice (compare 25:16). Nothing shows that "not good" stands for something far worse, and the two marks overlap.
"Will not go unpunished" is set against "will abound with blessings" as a firm assurance. It is a contrast, not plainly a lessened statement.

In "To show partiality is not good, yet a man will do wrong for a piece of bread", line 2's "do wrong" is no stronger than "not good". The verse shows no gap between what is said and what is meant, so the figure is not plain.
"Creatures of little power" (Hebrew "a people not mighty") simply describes small, weak animals, like the ants in 30:25, before setting their wisdom against it. It is not saying less to mean more.
"I have not spoken in secret" is a plain denial, followed by "I, the LORD, speak the truth". It is not understatement.
"From the beginning I have not spoken in secret" is a plain statement that God spoke openly. No understatement is visible.
The BSB reads "walk in the wrong path". "Wrong" says nothing less than is meant, so a BSB reader sees no understatement.

"something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind" is a strong denial, and the added clause makes it stronger. Reading "never commanded" as meaning "strictly forbade" needs other passages, so the verse does not plainly show understatement.
"something I never commanded or mentioned, nor did it even enter My mind" builds up a denial. Nothing in the verse shows it says less than it means.

The whole verse is marked. The only possible figure, "they are of no benefit at all to these people", can be read as a flat denial of the benefit the false prophets claim, and "at all" makes it more emphatic. That is doubtful, so it is dropped.
"how could you possibly go unpunished? You will not go unpunished" is a repeated, emphatic certainty of judgment. It does not say less than it means.
"will by no means leave you unpunished" is an emphatic assurance ("by no means"). It is not plainly saying less to mean more.
"something I never commanded them, nor had it ever entered My mind" is a strong denial, and the verse goes on to call it "such an abomination". It is not plainly understatement.
"will by no means leave you unpunished" is emphatic, as in 30:11. It is not a lessened statement.
"You will not go unpunished, for you must drink it too" answers the question before it with certainty. It is emphatic, not understatement.
The BSB reads "did what was wrong among his people". Plain "wrong" shows no understatement in the English, even though the Hebrew reads "not good".

"statutes that were not good and ordinances by which they could not live" is a disputed hard saying, and reading it as understatement is an interpretation, not plain. The marks also overlap ("were not good" sits inside "that were not good"), and "they could not" leaves out "live".
The BSB reads "wicked deeds", which is a plain statement, not an understatement.
"the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished" is an emphatic statement of God's justice. It does not say less than it means.

Reading "will not break" as meaning "will restore" needs an interpreter, so understatement is not plain. But the verse plainly pictures the weak and faltering as "A bruised reed" and "a smoldering wick" without naming them, which is a likeness implied (hypocatastasis). The marks move to those two pictures.
"the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven" is a plain, literal statement set against "every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven". It is not understatement.
"You are not far from the kingdom of God" may simply mean near but not yet in. The verse does not plainly show that less is said than meant.
"will not be forgiven" is a plain, literal statement set against "will be forgiven". Nothing is said less than is meant.
"ou pollas hemeras" (not many days) just means "a few days", as the BSB gives it. Nothing lessened is then made greater, so understatement is doubtful. The whole verse is also marked.
"ou pollas hemeras" is the ordinary Greek way to say "a few days" (the BSB's words), with no stronger point made. It is too doubtful to go live, and the whole verse is marked.
"ou meta pollas tautas hemeras" means "in a few days". It is the same "not many days" idiom, and it is not plain that less is said to mean more. The whole verse is also marked.
Plain narrative about Simon's sorcery and his boast. Nothing in it says less than it means, and the whole verse is marked.

"not left Himself without testimony" (ouk amarturon) denies a negative to affirm a rich witness, which the verse goes on to list: rain, fruitful seasons, food and gladness. The tags on ouk and amarturon are right. The span must take in "testimony".
The BSB reads "they spent a long time there", which is a plain statement with no understatement in the English.
The BSB reads "engaging these men in sharp debate", which states the matter directly with no understatement.
"quite a few leading women" is ordinary English for a fair number. A careful BSB reader would not see a figure here.
"quite a few prominent Greek women and men" is an ordinary English expression, not a plain understatement in the BSB.

"though He is not far from each one of us" works as a plain concession that God can be found. It is not clearly saying less to mean more, the way "no small stir" does. Reading it as understatement for force takes an interpretive step, so in doubt it is dropped.

"ou tas tuchousas" (not the ordinary) is understatement in the Greek, but the G3588 tag also marks the unrelated articles before "theos" and "cheiron". With the tags taken away, the BSB's "extraordinary miracles" shows no understatement, so the place cannot stand.
The BSB reads "a great disturbance", which is a direct statement and the opposite of an understatement.
The BSB reads "bringing much business to the craftsmen", which is a direct statement with no understatement.
"met' ou polu" ("it was not long before") is the ordinary idiom for "soon" and makes no stronger point. Like "not many days", it is too doubtful to go live, and the whole verse is marked.
The BSB reads "the great storm continued to batter us", which is direct, not understated.

"ou ten tuchousan philanthropian" (not the ordinary kindness) is understatement in the Greek, but G3588 also tags the unrelated articles (hoi, ton, ton, to). With the tags taken away, the BSB's "extraordinary kindness" shows no understatement, so the place cannot stand.
Nothing is understated. The BSB's two lines, "whose lawless acts are forgiven" and "whose sins are covered", say the same thing in other words. The marked words are those two whole lines.
"Your boasting is not good" may be a restrained way of saying it is shameful, but it reads just as well as a plain verdict. It is too doubtful to go live.
"the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God" is a plain, literal warning that verse 10 repeats. It is not understatement.
"I have no praise to offer" is a pointed contrast with 11:2, and the verse itself says outright "your gatherings do more harm than good". Understatement is not plain.
"I do not want you to be uninformed" is a set way of opening a subject. A careful reader would not plainly see it as saying less than is meant, and when in doubt the place is dropped.

"His grace to me was not in vain. No, I worked harder than all of them" states the "more" behind the lessened words, and the BSB itself shows it. G3756 also tags the second "ouk" ("yet not I"), which is not part of the figure, so the tags go.
"your labor in the Lord is not in vain" most likely just denies the futility raised in 15:14 and 15:17 ("in vain", "futile"). Nothing in the verse plainly shows that more is meant.

The plain denials are not understatement (the search's note leans on a commentary). But the three short clauses stand side by side with no "and", which the BSB plainly shows. Only those clauses should be marked, not "Make room for us in your hearts".
"our visit to you was not in vain" can be read as understatement, but the plain sense "not empty" fits just as well, and verse 2 only adds the bold preaching. It is too doubtful to go live.

"I am not ashamed" answers the command in 1:8 ("do not be ashamed of the testimony") and reads as a literal statement about real shame in suffering. The verse does not plainly show that less is said than meant.

"was unashamed of my chains" is set literally against those who deserted Paul (1:15) and carries on the chapter's theme of shame. It is not plainly an understatement, and the marked span is the whole verse anyway.

"Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers" reads naturally as a straight denial that He disowns them. It might be read as His glad welcome, but the verse does not plainly show that, so it is too doubtful with no writer behind it.

"do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize" is a double negative meaning one who fully sympathizes, and the verse itself spells out the stronger truth: "we have one who was tempted in every way that we are". The old span stopped at "unable", before the words that complete the figure.
places.words_why: "we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize ... but we have one who was tempted in every way": the double negative plainly understates. "with our weaknesses" is not needed to show it.
"God is not unjust. He will not forget your work": "not unjust" plainly says less than God's perfect justice. The verb "is" is not part of the figure.

places.why: "do not neglect to do good and to share" is an ordinary negative command, like 13:2. Nothing in the verse shows that less is said than meant, and the span breaks off before "good".

"they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive" reads at face value as these qualities guarding against fruitlessness. The understatement is not plain in the BSB wording, so the place is dropped.
